newsitem.title: BRAZIL: BRAZIL CONGRESS WEEK-Gov't seeking action, at last.
newsitem.headline: BRAZIL CONGRESS WEEK-Gov't seeking action, at last.

text.p: Brazil's Congress starts an extraordinary session to run through the July recess this week to make up for time lost on key pieces of legislation, including the government's centerpiece civil service and pension reforms.
Newspapers quoted government whips in the Chamber of Deputies sounding upbeat about the chances of finally pressing ahead with voting on outstanding amendments to the civil service reform bill.

"The moment has come to see if we have a majority or not," deputy Aecio Neves, the lower house leader of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's Brazilian Social Democratic Party (PSDB), told O Estado de Sao Paulo daily.
But whips have been saying things like that for more than two months only to call off votes on several amendments to the civil service bill which, if approved would make a mockery of the reform.
One proposed change would allow public sector workers to keep their lifetime job guarantees.

With many lawmakers unwilling to vote down the privileges of friends and supporters in the civil service, the government fears it might not muster the three-fifths majorities needed to kill the amendments.
Last week, officials said they hoped the triple pay of $23,000 each deputy and senator stands to gain in the July session might inspire the lawmakers to action.
The government's pension reform bill may be put to a long-awaited vote in a Senate committee later this week.

The bill has been rewritten to include several crucial points defeated in the Chamber of Deputies last year. It is considered sufficient to stem a growing deficit in the national social security system, set to reach about $1.0 billion in 1997.
Other items on an official agenda for the extraordinary session -- which runs until July 25 -- include a bill extending the government's Fiscal Stabilization Fund (FEF) until 1999.

The fund, which is due to expire Monday but may be extended retroactively once the bill is approved, allows the federal government to keep about $25 billion in receipts earmarked for states and municipalities. The money is used to cover shortfalls in the federal budget.

The bill was approved last week in a lower house committee and may be put to a first of two votes on the floor of the Chamber of Deputies Wednesday. As a constitutional amendment, it requires two three-fifths majorities in each house of Congress.

In the Senate, bills regulating the opening up of Brazil's massive telecommunications and petroleum industries are also scheduled for votes in July. Both bills have already been approved in the Chamber of Deputies.
Another pressing piece of legislation is a law which would set down the rules for next year's presidential, congressional and state governorship elections and which must be approved by early October.

Many observers expect the government to combine the October 1998 elections with a referendum on a possible "revisory" session of Congress which would make constitutional reform less difficult to implement.

In a revisory session, the constitution can be changed with simple majorities, far easier to get than the three-fifths majorities usually needed and which have frustrated the government in its two-year battle for civil service and pension reform.
